summary: Sets out procedures for modifying the Resource reSerVation Protocol (RSVP). It also provides new assignment guidelines for the number spaces used for RSVP messages, object classes, class-types, and sub-objects.

eli5.summary: It is the rulebook for how anyone is allowed to change a reservation system for network traffic, and for handing out new numbers and labels fairly.

questions: what is expert review in iana
what is a vendor private range
subtitle: The rulebook for who may change RSVP and how new message types, object classes and error codes get their numbers.

tldr.problem: RSVP gets extended over time, and its number spaces (message types, object classes, error codes and so on) needed clear rules so extensions are reviewed before code points are handed out.
tldr.mechanism: Each RSVP number space is split into ranges assigned by Standards Action, Expert Review, or Organization/Vendor Private use, and changes to procedures must be documented in a matching kind of RFC.
tldr.outcome: Extensions get review proportional to how settled they are, and vendor-private values can coexist through enterprise codes. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 96) that updates RFC 2205 and RFC 3209.

today: RFC 3936 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 96) published in October 2004. It updates RFC 2205 and RFC 3209, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Goals
sections.content:
This memo gives procedures for modifying the Resource reSerVation Protocol (RSVP): adding, updating, extending or obsoleting messages, object classes, header formats, error codes, and the procedures for sending, receiving and addressing RSVP messages.

IANA recognizes these RSVP name spaces: Message Types, Class Names, Class Numbers, Class Types and Sub-objects, Virtual Destination Ports, and Error Codes and (Subcode) Values. The memo sets ranges and assignment policies for each. New RSVP name spaces must be defined in a Standards Track RFC that includes IANA guidelines.

The aim is that extensions get adequate review before code points are assigned, without being overly rigid. It also updates the IANA Considerations section (section 7) of RFC 3209, replacing the policies stated there.
sections.eli5: When people want to add something new to the reservation system, there must be fair rules so changes are checked first but not blocked for no reason.

sections.title: The Three Assignment Policies
sections.content:
Each number space is divided into ranges, and each range uses one of three policies.

  • Standards Action, as defined in RFC 2434: needs a Standards Track RFC. Suited to widely accepted extensions whose ramifications are well understood.
  • Expert Review: values reviewed by an Expert designated by the IESG, typically for experimental extensions. Such assignments MUST be requested by Experimental RFCs documenting their use and processing, and the values MUST be registered with IANA.
  • Organization/Vendor Private: enterprise-specific values that MUST NOT be registered with IANA. The first 4-octet word of the data MUST be an enterprise code from the IANA SMI Network Management Private Enterprise Codes, so different vendors or standards bodies can use the same code point without collision.

A standards body other than the IETF must pick which kind of space it wants and submit the matching documentation. For a Standards Action space, a Standards Track RFC MUST be submitted.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of doors for getting a new number. One needs a big vote, one needs a single expert's okay, and one is a private door where each company adds its own name tag first.

sections.title: Message Types, Class Numbers and Class Types
sections.content:
A Message Type is an 8-bit number. Values 0 through 239 go by Standards Action and 240 through 255 by Expert Review.

Each object class has a Class Name and an 8-bit Class Number, split into three ranges by the two high-order bits. In each range the Standards Action, Expert Review and Vendor Private blocks are laid out as in the table below. A Vendor Private object must begin with the vendor's SMI enterprise code in network octet order. If an implementation does not recognize the code, it MUST handle the object and its message based on the Class-Num, as specified in RFC 2205, section 3.10.

Within a class, an 8-bit Class Type is scoped to the Class Number. Any new Class Number definition must say how additional Class Types are assigned. For the pre-existing Class Numbers the default is Standards Action unless a Standards Track or BCP RFC supersedes it.

Sub-objects of EXPLICIT_ROUTE (7-bit Type) and RECORD_ROUTE (8-bit Type) also get ranges. The first four octets of a Vendor Private sub-object MUST be the vendor's SMI enterprise code.
sections.eli5: Every kind of message and every kind of label has a number. The number line is cut into a part for official things, a part for experiments and a part for private company use.

sections.title: Error Codes and Virtual Destination Ports
sections.content:
An Error Code is an 8-bit value in the ERROR_SPEC object that broadly defines an error. It may come with a 16-bit Error Value giving more detail. Codes 0 through 239 are Standards Action, 240 through 251 are Expert Review and 252 through 255 are Vendor Private. For a Vendor Private code, the first four octets after the Error Value MUST be the vendor's SMI enterprise code. Globally defined Error Values are assigned by Standards Action.

Virtual destination ports are described in RFC 2207, which also specifies how IANA assigns them.
sections.eli5: Error numbers follow the same three-door idea. Numbers for private use start with the company's name tag so errors are never mixed up.

sections.title: Changing Procedures
sections.content: Each RSVP entity has procedures for when and how it is sent, received, processed and answered. A change to a procedure affecting an entity in a Standards Action range MUST be documented in a Standards Track RFC. A change affecting an entity in an Expert Review range MUST be documented in an Experimental RFC.
sections.eli5: If you change how an official thing works, you need an official write-up. If you change an experimental thing, an experimental write-up is enough.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content: The security section is short and hopeful: the procedures are meant to ensure that changes to RSVP are better reviewed and so more architecturally sound, which should improve the security of the protocol and of networks deploying it. The IANA Considerations section simply points to section 2.
sections.eli5: Checking changes carefully first makes it less likely that a new idea breaks something or opens a hole.
